reviews.meaning: Use reversible row operations to remove coefficients and expose a linear system's solutions.
reviews.definition: Elimination uses row swaps, nonzero scaling and adding a multiple of a different row. Applied to whole augmented rows, these preserve the solutions. Forward elimination clears entries below successive pivots to reach echelon form. Normalizing pivots and clearing above them produces reduced row echelon form (RREF).
reviews.conditions: Work over a field; these examples use exact rational numbers. Never divide by zero. Update every column, including the right-hand value. A pivot is the first nonzero entry of a nonzero echelon row.
reviews.change: The original summary was broadly correct but omitted the allowed operations, their restrictions and the stopping forms. Some texts use Gaussian elimination for the full reduction to RREF.
reviews.example:
[1,2|4] [3,5|11]
R2 <- R2 - 3 R1
[1,2|4] [0,-1|-1]
This is echelon form. Back-substitution gives y=1, x=2.

lesson.title: Why row elimination works
lesson.reading: The example replaces row two with row two minus three copies of row one. It clears the first coefficient of row two while preserving the original solutions.

tokens.role: One whole-row elimination step in the separate example.

reviews.meaning: RREF is a precisely defined final matrix form. Its uniqueness does not mean that a system has exactly one solution.
reviews.definition: Zero rows follow all nonzero rows. Each nonzero row starts with 1; these leading 1s move strictly right as you go down. Each leading 1 is the only nonzero entry in its column. For a fixed matrix over a field, the RREF is unique even when different legal operation sequences produce it.
reviews.conditions: Include the augmented column when checking the form. A row [0,0|1] means no solution. A consistent system with a free variable has multiple solutions over the rationals. A consistent system with a pivot for every variable has one solution.
reviews.change: The original uniqueness statement needed the defining conditions and the distinction between a unique matrix form and a unique solution. RREF does not require a square or invertible matrix.

lesson.title: What reduced form means
lesson.reading: This example is in RREF and has x=2, y=1. RREF can also describe an inconsistent system or a system with free variables; the unique form alone does not guarantee a unique solution.

tokens.role: Each variable column has a leading 1, with zero in the other row.

reviews.meaning: Rank counts independent columns. Comparing the ranks of A and [A|b] tells whether Ax=b has a solution.
reviews.definition: For a matrix A over a field, rank(A) is the dimension of its column space. It also equals the dimension of its row space and the number of pivots after row reduction. In Ax=b, A contains only the variable coefficients; [A|b] includes the right-hand column. The system is consistent (has at least one solution) exactly when rank(A)=rank([A|b]).
reviews.conditions: For m equations in n unknowns, A has m rows and n columns; b is not an unknown. Appending b leaves the rank unchanged exactly when b lies in the column space of A. If consistent, rank(A)=n gives one solution; rank(A)<n gives n-rank(A) free variables and infinitely many solutions over the rationals or reals. A reduced augmented row [0,...,0|c] with c nonzero means no solution, even if A has a pivot in every variable column.
reviews.change: The original column-space definition is correct but too brief to connect rank to solving. This adaptation adds the row/pivot interpretations and distinguishes coefficient rank from augmented rank. The equality-of-ranks criterion follows from the cited column-span consistency criterion: adding b changes the span dimension precisely when b is outside it.
reviews.example:
[1,2|3] [2,4|7]
R2 <- R2 - 2 R1 gives [1,2|3] [0,0|1].
rank(A)=1; rank([A|b])=2: no solution.
Change 7 to 6: both ranks are 1, with infinitely many rational solutions.

lesson.title: Rank and consistency
lesson.reading: Compare coefficient rank r=rank(A) with rank([A|b]). Unequal ranks: no solution. Equal ranks: the system is consistent. For n unknowns, r=n then gives one solution; r<n gives infinitely many over the rationals or reals. The column after | holds b, not another unknown. In the separate example, changing 7 to 6 removes the contradiction.

tokens.role: One coefficient pivot remains after eliminating the dependent second row.
The extra pivot in the right-hand column signals the contradiction 0=1.

reviews.meaning: Nullity counts independent directions that A sends to zero, and the free parameters available when Ax=b is consistent.
reviews.definition: For an m by n matrix A over a field, its kernel (null space) is the set of vectors x with Ax=0. Nullity is the dimension of that space. Rank-nullity says rank(A)+nullity(A)=n, the number of coefficient columns. In a consistent system, variables whose columns have no pivot in echelon form are free: they may be chosen independently, and the pivot variables follow from the equations.
reviews.conditions: The formula uses the finite dimension of the domain: n unknowns, excluding the augmented column. For consistent Ax=b, every solution is a particular solution plus a vector in the kernel; n-rank(A) counts its free parameters. Nullity(A) remains defined if Ax=b is inconsistent, but then there is no solution family to parameterize. A positive nullity gives infinitely many solutions only over an infinite field such as the rationals or reals, and only when consistent.
reviews.change: The original kernel definition and rank-nullity identity are correct for a finite-dimensional linear map, but omit that assumption and what dim V counts. This adaptation makes the matrix domain explicit and connects nonpivot variable columns to free parameters, without treating the right-hand column as a variable or promising solutions for an inconsistent system.
reviews.example:
[1,0,2|5] [0,1,-1|1]
rank(A)=2; nullity(A)=3-2=1.
z=t; x=5-2t; y=1+t.
All rational solutions: (5,1,0)+t(-2,1,1).
The kernel is spanned by (-2,1,1).

lesson.title: Nullity and free variables
lesson.reading: Here x and y have pivots; z does not. Choose any rational t for z, then x=5-2t and y=1+t. This describes every solution of the separate example. Its three coefficient columns and two pivots leave one free parameter. The last column supplies 5 and 1; it does not add an unknown. Check consistency before describing a solution family.

tokens.role: Three unknowns minus two coefficient pivots leave one kernel direction.
The nonpivot variable is free. Choosing t determines x and y through the displayed equations.
